1	# May 30, 2012 Meeting Transcript
     2	
     3	June 20, 2012
     4	
     5	UNITED STATES OF AMERICA  
     6	DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE
     7	
     8	COMMERCE SPECTRUM MANAGEMENT  
     9	ADVISORY COMMITTEE (CSMAC)
    10	
    11	MEETING
    12	
    13	WEDNESDAY  
    14	MAY 30, 2012
    15	
    16	The Advisory Committee met in Room 4830, Herbert C. Hoover Building, 1401 Constitution Avenue, N.W., Washington, D.C., at 10:00 a.m., Brian Fontes, Chair, presiding.
    17	
    18	## Members Present:
    19	
    20	Dr. Brian Fontes, Chief Executive Officer,  
    21	National Emergency Number Association, Chair
    22	
    23	Dr. David E. Borth, Independent Consultant
    24	
    25	Michael C. Calabrese, Vice President and  
    26	Director, Wireless Future Program, The  
    27	New America Foundation
    28	
    29	Thomas S. Dombrowsky, Jr., Engineering  
    30	Consultant, Wiley Rein, LLP
    31	
    32	David L. Donovan, President, Association for Maximum Service Television, Inc.*
    33	
    34	Margaret (Molly) Feldman, Vice President of Business Development, Verizon Wireless*
    35	
    36	Dr. Harold Furchtgott-Roth, President  
    37	Furchtgott-Roth Enterprises
    38	
    39	H. Mark Gibson, Director, Business  
    40	Development, Comsearch
    41	
    42	Dale N. Hatfield, Executive Director,  
    43	Center for Law Technology and  
    44	Entrepreneurship, University of  
    45	Colorado*
    46	
    47	Dr. Kevin C. Kahn, Technology Policy  
    48	Consultant, Intel
    49	
    50	Doug Mcginnis, IT Manager of Communication Infrastructure Strategy, Exelon Corporation*
    51	
    52	Dr. Mark A. Mchenry, President, Shared  
    53	Spectrum Company
    54	
    55	## Members Present:
    56	
    57	Janice Obuchowski, Founder and President, Freedom Technologies, Inc.
    58	
    59	Carl Povelites, Assistant Vice President of  
    60	Public Policy, AT&T
    61	
    62	Richard (Rick) Reaser, Jr., Head, Spectrum Management Department, Raytheon Space & Airborne Systems*
    63	
    64	Dr. Charles Rush, CMR Consulting
    65	
    66	Dr. Daniel Dean Stancil, Head, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, North Carolina State University*
    67	
    68	Bryan Tramont, Esq., Managing Partner,  
    69	Wilkinson Barker Knauer, LLP
    70	
    71	Jennifer Warren, Vice President, Technology Policy & Regulation, Lockheed Martin Corporation
    72	
    73	## Also Present:
    74	
    75	Karl Nebbia, Associate Administrator for  
    76	the Office of Spectrum Management
    77	
    78	Tom Power, White House Office of Science  
    79	and Technology Policy
    80	
    81	Larry Strickling, Assistant Secretary of  
    82	Commerce for Communications and Information
    83	
    84	Bruce M. Washington, Designated Federal  
    85	Officer
    86	
    87	\* Present via telephone
    88	
    89	## Contents
    90	
    91	[Welcome and Opening Remarks](#welcome)  
    92	[Opening Comments](#comments)  
    93	[Overview of 1755-1850 Report](#overview)  
    94	[Government/Industry Interaction](#interaction)  
    95	[Schedule of Next Meeting](#schedule)
    96	
    97	## Proceedings
    98	
    99	(10:03 a.m.)
   100	
   101	### Welcome and Opening Remarks {#welcome}
   102	
   103	Chair Fontes:  Good morning.  Before we begin, I'd just like to make sure that those who are on the phone who are committee members, if they could identify themselves.
   104	
   105	Member McGinnis:  Doug McGinnis from Exelon.
   106	
   107	Member Hatfield:  Dale Hatfield, University of Colorado.
   108	
   109	Member Feldman:  Molly Feldman, Verizon Wireless.
   110	
   111	Member Stancil:  Dan Stancil, NC State.
   112	
   113	Chair Fontes:  If we could only have the members themselves identify themselves, please.
   114	
   115	Asst. Sec. Strickling:  Only the committee members, please.
   116	
   117	Member Reaser:  Yes.  This is Rick Reaser at Raytheon.  I was wondering if you could ask everyone who is, like, on the phone call to mute when they're not talking, just as a courtesy.
   118	
   119	Chair Fontes:  That would be helpful.  Is that all of the committee members on the call?
   120	
   121	Member Donovan:  David Donovan with the New York State Broadcasters.
   122	
   123	Chair Fontes:  Thanks.  Great.  I believe we have all the committee members identified who are on the call.  I'd just like to go around the table if we could just to identify ourselves so the folks that are on the call will know what committee member --
   124	
   125	Male Participant:  I just joined the call.
   126	
   127	Chair Fontes:  Who is this?  I'm sorry.
   128	
   129	(Laughter.)
   130	
   131	Chair Fontes:  Okay.  I'm not really sure what's going on with the audio here, but if we can just go around and introduce ourselves.
   132	
   133	Member McHenry:  Mark McHenry with Shared Spectrum Company.
   134	
   135	Member Obuchowski:  Janice Obuchowski at FTI.
   136	
   137	Member Povelties:  Carl Povelites, AT&T.
   138	
   139	Member Rush:  Charles Rush, CMR Consulting.
   140	
   141	Member Tramont:  Bryan Tramont, Wilkinson Barker.
   142	
   143	Member Borth:  Dave Borth, University of Illinois and independent consultant.
   144	
   145	Mr. Nebbia:  Karl Nebbia, NTIA.
   146	
   147	Chair Fontes:  Brian Fontes, CSMAC.
   148	
   149	Asst. Sec. Strickling:  Larry Strickling, NTIA.
   150	
   151	Mr. Power:  Tom Power, Office of Science and Technology Policy.
   152	
   153	Member Warren:  Jennifer Warren, Lockheed Martin.
   154	
   155	Member Dombrowsky:  Tom Dombrowsky, Wiley Rein.
   156	
   157	Member Furchtgott-Roth:  Harold Furchtgott-Roth, Furchtgott-Roth Economics.
   158	
   159	Member Gibson:  Mark Gibson, Comsearch.
   160	
   161	Member Kahn:  Kevin Kahn, Intel.
   162	
   163	Chair Fontes:  Great.  Again, I'd just like to remind those who are on the call if they're not speaking to put the phone on mute, that will help everybody who is participating on the phone and here in person.
   164	
   165	I'd like to just welcome everyone this morning.  I'd like to turn it over now to Larry Strickling.
   166	
   167	### Opening Comments {#comments}
   168	
   169	Asst. Sec. Strickling:  Thank you, Brian.  I'll be quick.  I just want to welcome everyone here today.  I just want to tell those of you who felt that CSMAC wasn't working hard enough, who felt that you weren't working on the most relevant issues, that you weren't getting your name in the headlines, we've listened to you, and today I'm actually quite excited to have Karl roll out today what I hope will be a very exciting new work effort under the auspices of CSMAC to really take on, in a serious and intensive way, this question of facilitating sharing between commercial and agency spectrum operations.
   170	
   171	So there really is a ton of work to get done.  Karl has laid out a plan for how we're going to organize to do this within the CSMAC framework and I hope all of you are as excited to get involved in this new effort as we are to have you all involved in this.
   172	
   173	So with that, I'm just going to turn the mic over to Tom Power from the White House.
   174	
   175	Mr. Power:  Thanks, Larry, and good morning.  I really just wanted to thank you all and congratulate you all for rolling up your sleeves and getting down to this important business of figuring out how the commercial industry and federal users can share the 1755 band.
   176	
   177	It was two and a half years ago that the Obama administration concluded that re-purposing 500 MHZ of spectrum from existing uses, both commercial or federal, to wireless broadband was the goal within ten years.  And that was later memorialized in the President's memorandum that the President issued in June 2010, just about two years ago.
   178	
   179	And with that direction, NTIA and the agencies really got down to work to figure out how to get to that goal.  We've been getting together every couple of weeks for a few hours downstairs in our windowless, but cool, room to, sort of, map out our plans and see where we are.
   180	
   181	And that's in addition to the individual teams within the agencies that are doing work on their own.  Within six months of that memorandum, NTIA and the agencies have identified 115 MHz of spectrum that could be turned over for wireless broadband and make that available for the FCC to start their work in planning on how that could be made available, and then got to work on the 1755 band.
   182	
   183	When we looked back at that memorandum, though, one of the words that jumped out is sharing, because two years ago, we recognized that that was an important piece of the puzzle here.  I think it's pretty clear whether you're a federal agency or a commercial provider, sharing is probably not the first option you would jump to in a perfect world, not because we all revert to childhood and that reaction when mom told you to share with your brother.  Was that TMI?
   184	
   185	(Laughter.)
   186	
   187	Asst. Sec. Strickling:  But in your case, it's --
   188	
   189	Mr. Power:  But really because exclusive access, if nothing else, brings you certainty.  It's just a little bit easier to deal when you know you only have yourself to worry about and that's a good thing.  And whether you're trying to plan to protect our training for our pilots, or got unnamed vehicles in the air, or tracks of your weather, or how to invest and build broadband networks to satisfy the skyrocketing consumer demand for broadband, it sort of gives you a good thing.
   190	
   191	But we know two things.  One, spectrum is finite and two, we have compelling needs for spectrum on both sides of this equation, from the government side and from the commercial side.  And no one is saying that either of those sides should be ignored.  So that's why we're concentrating on sharing, just as the President called for two years ago.
   192	
   193	I know sharing can encompass a lot of approaches.  The FCC has gotten the T.V. White Spaces Program up and running, one way of having devices being able to find out what spectrum is available in the market that the device happens to be located in.
   194	
   195	Of course, there's a lot of work on cognitive radios and other dynamic spectrum technology so that you can, on a more of a real-time basis, figure out what frequencies are available or not available.
   196	
   197	And I guess some could say that sharing involves new architectures of the evolving trend in architectures with smaller cells, lower power, allowing greater re-use within a fixed geographic area.
   198	
   199	And I think for today's purposes, all those solutions, obviously, got to be a part of the answer here.  But I think for today's purposes, we really are going to be looking at a more refined focus on what the needs of the federal agencies are, the cost and opportunities involved in relocating versus staying put, what interference tolerance can really be accommodated, how can we accommodate co-existence into the bandwidth.
   200
